lesson.title: Building Lists: From Literals to Loops
lesson.summary: The several ways to bring a list into existence: typing it out directly, converting another sequence, or building one up piece by piece.
lesson.body:
Now that you know what a list is, the next question is how you actually get data into one. Sometimes you know every value ahead of time and can simply type them out. Other times the values come from somewhere else, a range of numbers, the characters of a string, or the results of a computation, and you need a way to turn that source into a list. Python supports both approaches, and knowing when to reach for each one will save you a lot of unnecessary typing.

The most direct method is a list literal: writing the values you want inside square brackets, separated by commas, exactly as you saw in the previous concept. An empty list is written as empty_list = [], which is a perfectly valid list with zero elements, useful as a starting point you plan to fill in later.

The list() constructor takes an existing sequence and converts it into a list. This is especially useful with range(), which produces a sequence of numbers but is not itself a list, and with strings, which are sequences of characters.

numbers = list(range(1, 6))
print(numbers)

letters = list("hello")
print(letters)

Trace the first example carefully: range(1, 6) produces the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, stopping before 6 because the stop value in range is always exclusive. Converting that to a list gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], which is exactly what prints. The second example converts the string "hello" into a list of its individual one-character strings, printing ['h', 'e', 'l', 'l', 'o']. Notice that list("hello") does not give you back the word hello as a single item; it splits the string into its five separate characters, since a string is itself just a sequence, and list() breaks any sequence into its individual elements.

A third technique, one you will use constantly once you start modifying lists, is building a list up dynamically: start with an empty list and add to it as you go, usually inside a loop. This pattern will become second nature once you learn the append method in an upcoming concept, but the shape of it is worth previewing now because it directly parallels the accumulator pattern from loops and recursion. You start empty, you repeat some action, and each repetition contributes one more piece to the final result, the same mental model as list_sum building up a total one call at a time.

Python also offers a more compact way to build a list from a computation, called a list comprehension, which packs a loop and an expression into a single line:

squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

Here Python evaluates x**2 for every x produced by range(1, 6), which is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, giving squared values 1, 4, 9, 16, and 25. The result printed is [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. You do not need to master list comprehensions immediately, but recognizing the pattern, a loop variable and an expression tucked inside brackets, will help you read other people's code long before you start writing your own. Whichever method you choose, the result is the same kind of object: an ordered list ready for indexing, slicing, and the methods covered later in this unit.
